extracted.intended_audience: regulated employers, legal counsel, policy stakeholders, and commenters on the FTC non‑compete rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble discussion of the Commission's legal authority, constitutional and administrative law defenses, jurisdictional scope, and the legal standard for what constitutes an unfair method of competition under section 5, as applied to a rule banning most non‑compete clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional ratification as evidence of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress fails for a long time to alter a judicial construction and later enacts legislation that implicitly recognizes that construction as effective, such inaction and subsequent legislation are persuasive evidence that Congress endorses the judicial construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission relies on the 1975 and 1980 amendments and long congressional inaction as confirmatory evidence that Congress understood and preserved the Commission's section 6(g) rulemaking power; quote: '[t]he long time failure of Congress to alter ... is persuasive of legislative recognition that the judicial construction is the correct one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory text authorizes rulemaking under section 6(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain text of the FTC Act grants the Commission authority 'to make rules and regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions' of the Act, including preventing 'unfair methods of competition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the statute speaks plainly, legislative history is unnecessary. The Commission emphasizes the statute's text and subsequent enacted amendments as providing unambiguous authority to promulgate substantive, economically significant rules under section 6(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of authority in 1975 and 1980 amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacted later amendments (1975, 1980) that preserved or presumed the Commission's rulemaking authority under section 6(g), reinforcing that Congress ratified the Commission's power to make substantive rules defining unfair methods of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission treats these amendments as congressional recognition and confirmation of the D.C. Circuit's construction that the Commission may promulgate legislative rules under section 6(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: rule applies only to entities within the Commission's jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule applies only to the extent the Commission has jurisdiction under the FTC Act; entities or activities explicitly exempted by the Act (e.g., banks, Packers and Stockyards Act coverage) are not covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission declines to restate every jurisdictional limit in the rule text because jurisdictional status can be fact‑specific; the FTC Act definition of 'person' and other statutory provisions govern applicability; the rule clarifies in §910.1 that it applies to legal entities within the Commission's jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 22 regulatory‑analysis triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22 of the FTC Act requires the Commission to perform a regulatory analysis for rule amendments that would have 'their annual effect on the national economy' or substantial effects on the national economy, prices, or regulated entities and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress anticipated the Commission's authority could have broad economic effects and set out procedural steps and checks for such rulemakings; the Commission cites §22 as evidence Congress contemplated economically significant rulemaking power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency asserts authority in an area of exceptional economic and political significance, courts require 'something more than a merely plausible textual basis' and often look for clear congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission concludes the non‑compete rule does not implicate the major questions doctrine because the Commission's asserted authority has substantial historical and statutory footing; even if major questions applied, the FTC Act 'declared unlawful' unfair methods and authorized rulemaking, which the Commission reads as clear authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑delegation (intelligible principle) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may delegate regulatory power so long as it lays down an 'intelligible principle' to guide the delegatee; broad delegations have been upheld where Congress sets policy boundaries or purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission treats the FTC Act's prohibition of 'unfair methods of competition' plus the Act's purpose and context as an intelligible principle; Supreme Court precedents (including Schechter Poultry discussion) support that this statutory scheme is a permissible delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) compliance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To promulgate a legislative rule under the APA, an agency must provide prior public notice, an opportunity to comment, and consider those comments before finalizing a rule; only final agency action is reviewable under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission states it complied with the APA, treated the NPRM as preliminary, reviewed and considered all comments, and made changes to the proposed rule where appropriate; commenters' failure to recognize the NPRM's preliminary nature does not mean APA noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce Clause compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress's Commerce Clause power permits regulation of 'commerce ... among the several States'; the FTC Act's phrase 'in or affecting commerce' is coextensive with that constitutional power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds use of non‑competes substantially affects commerce as defined in the FTC Act, and the final rule extends only to the full extent of the FTC's jurisdiction consistent with the Commerce Clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth Amendment and federalism limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges invoking the Tenth Amendment do not bar the rule so long as Congress acted within its Commerce Clause authority and the FTC's jurisdiction does not exceed that constitutional power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Congress granted the Commission authority under the Commerce Clause, the Commission concludes it is not intruding on powers reserved to the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts/rights to contract and rational‑basis review
rubrics_metrics.description: If a constitutional right to contract were implicated, substantive‑due‑process review would require only a rational basis for federal regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission asserts a rational relationship exists between the regulation of non‑competes and legitimate government purposes—preventing unfair methods of competition, promoting competition, and furthering innovation—satisfying rational‑basis scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness/doctrine of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation must provide regulated parties with sufficient notice of what the law demands; overly vague provisions can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission withdrew the proposed 'de facto' non‑competes language and clarified the final rule's definition of 'non‑compete clause,' explaining that whether a specific clause falls within the rule depends on precise language but that the text provides sufficient notice to satisfy due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑part test for 'unfair methods of competition' under section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 assessment requires (1) whether the conduct is a method of competition (not merely a market condition), and (2) whether it is unfair—i.e., goes beyond competition on the merits; the unfairness inquiry has two components (a) indicia of unfairness and (b) tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions, weighed on a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Commission's legal standard for evaluating conduct under section 5; the second prong does not require proof of actual anticompetitive effects, but an analysis of tendency and indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of unfairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that indicate unfairness include 'the extent to which the conduct may be coercive, exploitative, collusive, abusive, deceptive, predatory, or involve the use of economic power of a similar nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicia may also include restrictive or exclusionary qualities depending on commercial context and current/future effects; indicia are weighed along with tendency to harm competitive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions (second prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: This prong focuses on the nature and tendency of conduct to harm competitive conditions and does not require a detailed economic analysis or proof of actual harm; it asks whether the conduct tends to raise prices, reduce output, limit choice, lower quality, reduce innovation, impair or exclude market participants, reduce nascent competition, reduce labor mobility, suppress worker compensation, or degrade working conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry examines tendencies and plausible competitive effects rather than only concrete realized harms; these illustrative harms help evaluate the 'tendency' element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑part jurisdictional test for nonprofit entities
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether an entity claiming tax‑exempt nonprofit status falls within the FTC's jurisdiction, the Commission applies a two‑part test: (1) adequate nexus between the organization's activities and its alleged public purposes, and (2) whether net proceeds are properly devoted to recognized public (not private) interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission looks to both source of income (whether organized for and actually engaged in business for charitable purposes) and destination of income (whether the corporation or its members derive a profit); tax‑exempt status is a factor but not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors showing a purported nonprofit is within jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that a tax‑exempt claimant is subject to FTC jurisdiction include: engaging in business on behalf of for‑profit members, ceding effective control to a for‑profit partner (impermissible private benefit), paying unreasonable or percentage‑based compensation to insiders, or other private‑benefit arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission and judicial precedents (e.g., physician‑hospital organization, independent physician association) show organizations claiming tax‑exempt status were treated as within FTC jurisdiction where they provided pecuniary benefits to private actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking versus adjudication equivalence and procedural fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may determine that non‑competes are unfair via case‑by‑case adjudication or via rulemaking; rulemaking allows broader participation and may be fairer to parties than exclusive reliance on adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters conceded that adjudication could find specific non‑competes unlawful; the Commission defends using rulemaking to make the same type of determination in a general, transparent process with notice and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practice and precedent for economy‑wide rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has historically promulgated economy‑wide rules (e.g., Mail Order Rule, Negative Option Rule) under section 6(g) that applied across industries and were upheld by courts, demonstrating the long use of rulemaking authority to address broad unfair practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites past rulemakings and judicial affirmations (including the Seventh Circuit upholding the Mail Order Rule) as support that economy‑spanning rules are consistent with statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits on restating jurisdictional boundaries in rule text
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission will not attempt to restate or capture every potential jurisdictional interpretation or exclusion in the rule text because such an attempt could create confusion; jurisdictional determinations remain fact‑specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, the Commission relies on the FTC Act's definitions and existing jurisprudence to govern applicability and clarifies definitions (e.g., 'person' in §910.1) where appropriate.
